info.description:
**trixd** is the TrinityX daemon for everything that is not a physical node: the cluster's users and groups, the Prometheus monitoring configuration, starting and stopping services, and the slurm and genders files computed from Luna's node list. Every route below says what it does, what to send, what comes back, and who may call it.

**Luna**, luna2-daemon, runs beside it on this controller and owns the physical estate: nodes, groups, images, networks and boot. It answers at https://<controller>:7050, and [https://<controller>:7050/version](https://<controller>:7050/version) says which version it runs. A request to `/api/v1/luna/<path>` here is handed to Luna as `/<path>`, unchanged, and Luna decides who may.

### Signing in
1. `POST /api/v1/auth/token` with `{"username": "...", "password": "..."}` answers `201` and `{"token": "..."}`, valid for an hour unless `trixd.ini` says otherwise.
2. Send the token on every call as `x-access-tokens: <token>`, as Luna takes it, or as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.
3. On this page: **Authorize**, paste the token into either field, and every **Try it out** sends it.

### Who may call what
A user holds one role: `none` < `reader` < `operator` < `manager`. Each route admits a lowest role, shown as **Access** under its description. **rootus**, the account `trixd.ini` names, is the administrator and passes every check. `none` may only ask who it is, with `GET /api/v1/auth/whoami`.

### Ports
**8050** speaks the protocol `trixd.ini` names, https or http. **8051** is plain HTTP on every address, for nodes; a password or token sent there crosses the network in clear text.

### Errors
A refusal or a failure answers its status and `{"message": "..."}` saying why: 400 a request that cannot be acted on, 401 no token or a bad one, 403 a role below the route's minimum, 404 no such object, 409 a conflict, 422 a body that does not match its schema (FastAPI's `detail` list instead of `message`), 502 the service behind trixd failed, 503 not available on this controller.
info.title: TrinityX Daemon (trixd)

post.description:
How a node signs in after boot, on the terms Luna uses. When the cluster enforces security the node presents its TPM measurement, `tpm_sha256`, which must match what Luna holds for it; otherwise the daemon's own account, or one holding a role that may act for a node. Never on the node name alone, and never on being merely a known user: this token is the node's identity, and Luna honours it as such.

The token is confined to that node: it is accepted only on node routes for the node it names, such as `PATCH /api/v1/prometheus/hw-rules/{node}`.

**Access:** public, no token

get.description:
The baseline the installer rendered, what this site has defined on top of it, and every
scope that deviates. The baseline is a file and is NOT replicated, so its digest is
reported here: one call on each controller, and two different digests mean the pair
disagrees about what it is scraping while the database looks converged.

`read` says whether that file is the baseline in use. False means it is absent,
unreadable or names no nodes section, and the exporters built into the daemon are being
served instead - which two digests alone would not tell you.

`ignored` is what the last read of that file threw away: a label Prometheus will not
accept, a port that is not a number, a duration that is not one. The file is forgiving,
because one bad label must not cost a cluster its targets - this is where it says what
it forgave, rather than only a log line that has since rotated.

**Access:** reader or above: reader, operator, manager and rootus

get.description:
The Prometheus rule file trixd holds for one node, as YAML loads it: one group,
`trinityx_hw`, with one `MissingHardwareComponent` alert for each part `lshw` reported
when the file was generated. An alert fires when its part stops being reported, so a
missing DIMM, disk or card is noticed.

Each rule's labels say how its alert counts: `nhc`, whether it counts for the node's

Use this rather than `/system/notify` from anything inside another service's request, such as a hook: notify acts before it answers, and acting reads back from the source, so a source waiting on trixd would be waiting on itself.

Each change is named as `<source>.<object>.<event>` with whatever the source holds about it, exactly as `/system/notify` takes one. Send the whole set in one call: a caller with a hundred changed nodes makes one request, not a hundred.

get.description:
For a monitor, with no token. `plugins` counts the loaded plugins. Each render says when it last ran, as Unix time, 0 before its first run since trixd or its plugin started, and whether that run worked. `triggers` carries one entry per loaded trigger: `luna_hashes` says whether Luna answers its table hashes, which it does on an HA master only, and `replication` when the last sweep ran, 0 for never, with `not_converging` counting the peer and table pairs that have still differed after several passes - which means neither controller is taking the other's row. `owed` counts the replicated calls still waiting for a peer, the ones given up on, the peers configured and the peers not answering - counts only, and no peer is named, because this route takes no token: `GET /system/replication/owed` says where, and `oldest_pending` says in seconds how long the oldest waiting call has waited, which is what tells a busy queue from a stuck one. States and times only: an error's text stays in the log.

Every plugin that declared that event acts on it, and the renders that read the object run again. `payload` is whatever the source holds about the change and is passed on unchanged.

A plugin that declared nothing is not called, and an event nobody declared is not an error: `acted` then says so and the renders still run. Ring it once after a sweep rather than once per node; a whole set belongs in the plugin's own bulk route.

post.description:
The other controller made a call whose effect is not in a replicated table and which no render brings back - a hardware rule file written or retired, for instance - so it asks this controller to make the same call. Only an endpoint whose own manifest says `replicate` can be asked for, which is checked here as well as there, so a version-skewed pair refuses instead of being talked into work it does not declare.

The named handler is called directly rather than the route being re-entered, so nothing is written down to send onwards: there is no loop to prevent and no hop count to get wrong. rootus only, which is the account the pair already shares for replication.

Two conventions a replicating handler's answer carries. `skipped`, as a non-empty string, means the handler declined to act - the node is not in this controller's Luna, say - and the sender then treats the call as not done and offers it again rather than recording it as applied; it is a reserved key, and a count of skipped items must not use it. Offering the same call again is answered with the answer given the first time, since delivery is at-least-once and the sender waits three seconds.

**Access:** rootus only: the account trixd.ini names, and the other controller of a pair
